entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Marcius Philippus was a prominent politician and senator in the late Roman Republic, serving as governor of Syria from 61 to 60 BC and later in the consulship of 56 BC. As stepfather to the emperor Augustus, he played a pivotal role in shaping Roman politics and governance. His tenure as governor of Syria was marked by significant administrative reforms and military campaigns against the Parthian Empire.

Philippus's legacy extends beyond his own life, as he contributed to the development of the Roman administrative system, which would later influence the organization of the Roman Empire. His influence can be seen in the work of later Roman administrators, such as the emperor Vespasian, who built upon Philippus's reforms to create a more efficient and effective system.

Despite his significant impact on Roman politics, Philippus's own personal life remains somewhat of a mystery. Little is known about his early life or family, and his connections to other Roman leaders and figures are not well-documented.

A striking example of Philippus's influence can be seen in the laws and decrees he issued as governor of Syria, which have been preserved in ancient sources and offer valuable insights into the administrative practices of the Roman Empire during this period.

The Roman historian Tacitus would later write of Philippus's 'singular energy and industry' in his account of the Roman senatorial class, highlighting the importance of this figure in shaping the Roman Empire's governance and politics.
